say.text: A 58-year-old man has a routine ultrasound for a check-up. It shows a 1.5 cm gallstone. He has never had pain, fever or jaundice.
Does this stone need treatment now?

choices.label: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy now, to prevent later cancer
Expectant care, with review if symptoms begin
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) for six months, to dissolve it
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what this stone is doing to him right now, not what it could one day do.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting, since stones do cause cholecystitis, but most gallstones never cause symptoms, and symptoms start at only about 1–2% a year.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: the stone itself is not the indication, its behaviour is.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting, since UDCA is the tablet most people remember, but it works only on small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a working gallbladder, and stones return after stopping it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the stone and the gallbladder before you reach for the drug.

say.text: The key is expectant care, with no operation for a silent stone.
About 80% of gallstones are asymptomatic, and symptoms start at roughly 1–2% a year, so a silent stone alone is not an indication.
You act on symptoms or on a specific high-risk feature, not on the presence of a stone.

choices.label: A patient with a porcelain gallbladder and no symptoms

choices.label: A large calcified stone in a gallbladder that fills

Not sure, give me a hint

Fitness and critical illness set the plan, so B is drained first
B has no stone, so antibiotics alone are enough
Not sure, give me a hint

choices.label: Operate at once, since early surgery is the answer in every grade
Drainage cures the disease, so surgery is never needed
Organ dysfunction makes surgery unsafe until he is supported and drained
Not sure, give me a hint

The cystic duct is dissected down to the bile duct junction
Triangle cleared, and the lower gallbladder separated from the liver bed

Across laparoscopic cholecystectomies, what is the commonest cause of a major bile duct injury?

choices.label: Misidentifying the common bile duct as the cystic duct
Bleeding from the cystic artery, clipped blindly across the field
Injury to the right hepatic artery during dissection

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting, since bleeding is the event surgeons fear most, but bleeding is not the commonest route to a major duct injury.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting, since the right hepatic artery lies near the dissection, but injuring it is a vascular event, not the commonest cause of major duct injury.
The commonest cause is misidentification: the common bile duct is taken for the cystic duct and divided.
That is why the view must be confirmed before clipping, since the cystic artery is usually a branch of the right hepatic artery.
